title: The attributes
hook: one verse says nothing is like Him, and in the same breath calls Him the Hearer, the Seer

segments.voice: Yesterday, why suffering, and your line: not always seen. Did you leave a little room for a reason you couldn't see yet? Today, how to speak of the One we can't see. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-one.

One sentence of the Qur'an, in two halves. The first half, in Pickthall's translation: "Naught is as His likeness." Nothing is like Him. Full stop, it seems. Then, in the same breath: "and He is the Hearer, the Seer." Hearing and seeing are things you do. A child does them. A cat does them. So the same verse that says nothing is like Allah goes straight on to describe Him with words we use for ourselves. That isn't a slip. It's the whole problem of this part of the path in one line. Today, the attributes, and how to speak of them.
screen: `NAUGHT IS AS HIS LIKENESS.` → `AND HE IS THE HEARER, THE SEER.` → `BOTH IN ONE VERSE.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is sifat, attributes, the qualities Allah describes Himself with: knowing, willing, powerful, living, hearing, seeing, speaking. Another verse says: "Allah's are the fairest names. Invoke Him by them." So Muslims call on Him by what He has said of Himself. But how do you use those words without shrinking Him to our size? Theologians name two ditches on either side of the road. One is tashbih, likening: hearing like ours, only bigger, with ears and a place to stand. The other is ta'til, emptying out: deciding the words mean nothing at all. The road runs between. And the schools we've met this part each walk it their own way. The Atharis say: affirm hearing and seeing as they came, and don't ask how. The Ash'aris and Maturidis affirm a set of attributes as real and eternal, set out by argument, and explain some other descriptions with care. The Mu'tazilah, guarding oneness, said Allah knows and hears by His very essence, not by attributes added to Him. And Shia theology has its own careful version of that same concern. Different routes, one shared fence: He is not like His creation. One way theologians put it: He hears, but not with ears. He sees, but not with eyes. The word hearing is true of Him. The picture that comes with it isn't. That's where the verse leaves us: real names, real attributes, and nothing like Him.
screen: `SIFAT: WHAT HE SAYS OF HIMSELF.` · `TWO DITCHES: LIKENING, EMPTYING.` · `EACH SCHOOL WALKS THE ROAD.` · then, large: `HE HEARS, NOT WITH EARS.`

segments.voice: The practice: reflect on one attribute. Settle, and breathe. Listen. Count, loosely, the sounds you can hear: a fan, traffic, your own breath. Notice how few you can hold at once, and how much you miss in the next room. That's hearing, ours: limited, tired, needing ears. Now hold the word the verse uses: the Hearer. Don't build a picture. Let it be hearing without any of those limits, and without any of our shape. If you pray, you can call on Him by that name, as-Sami'. If you don't, let the phrase nothing like Him be enough. The bell holds the time.
Sifat. The attributes of Allah: hearing, seeing, knowing, willing and more, affirmed without likening Him to anything. Today's word.

Your line: nothing like him. Today, when you catch yourself picturing God as a bigger version of someone, set the picture down and keep the word. Tomorrow, the miracle of the Qur'an. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Muslims call on Allah by His names and attributes, such as as-Sami', the Hearer, and al-Basir, the Seer, while holding with Qur'an 42:11 that nothing is like Him; the schools of theology explain the attributes in different ways.

Qur'an 42:11 puts both halves in one sentence.

avoiding likening means saying the words mean nothing
theologians call that ta'til, the other ditch.

fork.setup: the Qur'an calls Allah the Hearer. how do the theologians want you to take it?
options: real hearing, but not with ears, and like nothing in creation.
just a figure of speech that means nothing.
fork.reveal: the verse holds both: nothing is like Him, and He is the Hearer. The schools differ in how they explain it, but all avoid likening Him to creation.

original.note: Arabic: attributes, qualities; the singular is sifa.

trapdoor: what you thought: if God hears and sees, He must have ears and eyes.
what it means: the attributes are real, but Allah is like nothing in creation, so the picture doesn't apply.
what a scholar hears: tashbih and ta'til on either side, and the schools' long debate over essence and attributes.
